claim: SKAP2 is required for protection against K. pneumoniae (ATCC 43816) pulmonary infections.
source: We show that the adaptor protein, SKAP2, is required for protection against K. pneumoniae (ATCC 43816) pulmonary infections.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing increased bacterial burden in Skap2-/- mice.

claim: Skap2-/- mice had 100-fold higher bacterial burden when compared to wild-type.
source: Skap2-/- mice had 100-fold higher bacterial burden when compared to wild-type and burden was controlled by SKAP2 expression in innate immune cells.
evidence: This is supported by CFU measurements shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1M.

claim: Bacterial burden was controlled by SKAP2 expression in innate immune cells.
source: Skap2-/- mice had 100-fold higher bacterial burden when compared to wild-type and burden was controlled by SKAP2 expression in innate immune cells.
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Skap2-/- neutrophils and monocytes were present in infected lungs.
source: Skap2-/- neutrophils and monocytes were present in infected lungs, and the neutrophils degranulated normally in response to K. pneumoniae infection in mice
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1C and histological examination in Figure 1D-L.

claim: Skap2-/- neutrophils degranulated normally in response to K. pneumoniae infection in mice.
source: Skap2-/- neutrophils and monocytes were present in infected lungs, and the neutrophils degranulated normally in response to K. pneumoniae infection in mice
evidence: This is supported by ELISA measurements of MMP-9 and ELA2 in Figure 4A-B.

claim: K. pneumoniae-stimulated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in vitro was abolished in Skap2-/- neutrophils.
source: however, K. pneumoniae-stimulated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production in vitro was abolished.
evidence: This is supported by isoluminol-chemiluminescence assays shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: K. pneumoniae-induced neutrophil ROS response required the activity of SFKs, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, and PKC.
source: K. pneumoniae-induced neutrophil ROS response required the activity of SFKs, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, and PKC.
evidence: This is supported by inhibitor studies shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The loss of SKAP2 significantly hindered the K. pneumoniae-induced phosphorylation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2.
source: The loss of SKAP2 significantly hindered the K. pneumoniae-induced phosphorylation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 implicating SKAP2 as proximal to their activation in pathogen-signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 5F-L.

claim: SKAP2 is implicated as proximal to the activation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 in pathogen-signaling pathways.
source: The loss of SKAP2 significantly hindered the K. pneumoniae-induced phosphorylation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 implicating SKAP2 as proximal to their activation in pathogen-signaling pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced phosphorylation of these kinases in Skap2-/- neutrophils.

claim: SKAP2-dependent signaling in neutrophils is essential for K. pneumoniae-activated ROS production.
source: In conclusion, SKAP2-dependent signaling in neutrophils is essential for K. pneumoniae-activated ROS production and for promoting bacterial clearance during infection.
evidence: This is supported by the abolishment of ROS production in Skap2-/- neutrophils shown in Figure 5.

claim: SKAP2-dependent signaling in neutrophils is essential for promoting bacterial clearance during infection.
source: In conclusion, SKAP2-dependent signaling in neutrophils is essential for K. pneumoniae-activated ROS production and for promoting bacterial clearance during infection.
evidence: This is supported by the increased bacterial burden in Skap2-/- mice and the rescue by WT bone marrow cells.

claim: K. pneumoniae is an opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen that can cause a wide range of life-threatening infections, including pneumonia, sepsis and urinary tract infections.
source: Klebsiella pneumoniae is an opportunistic Gram-negative pathogen that can cause a wide range of life-threatening infections, including pneumonia, sepsis and urinary tract infections (Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa, 2019; Paczosa and Mecsas, 2016; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2018; Weiner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: K. pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-associated infections.
source: K. pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-associated infections with one recent study reporting that K. pneumoniae contributes to 7.7% of cases from over 4500 hospitals (Weiner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weiner et al., 2016.

claim: K. pneumoniae contributes to 7.7% of hospital-associated infection cases from over 4500 hospitals.
source: K. pneumoniae is a leading cause of hospital-associated infections with one recent study reporting that K. pneumoniae contributes to 7.7% of cases from over 4500 hospitals (Weiner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weiner et al., 2016.

claim: The increasing number of severe K. pneumoniae infections are largely attributed to a rise in antibiotic-resistant strains.
source: The increasing number of severe, and sometimes systemic, K. pneumoniae infections are largely attributed to a rise in antibiotic-resistant strains (Falagas et al., 2014; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2018; Kobayashi et al., 2016) and hypervirulent strains that generate thicker capsules (Zhang et al., 2016; Harada et al., 2019; Lam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The increasing number of severe K. pneumoniae infections are largely attributed to hypervirulent strains that generate thicker capsules.
source: The increasing number of severe, and sometimes systemic, K. pneumoniae infections are largely attributed to a rise in antibiotic-resistant strains (Falagas et al., 2014; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2018; Kobayashi et al., 2016) and hypervirulent strains that generate thicker capsules (Zhang et al., 2016; Harada et al., 2019; Lam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Neutropenic patients are highly susceptible to life-threatening respiratory and bloodstream infections, including those caused by K. pneumoniae.
source: Highlighting the importance of the innate immune response, neutropenic patients are highly susceptible to life-threatening respiratory and bloodstream infections, including those caused by K. pneumoniae (Zhu et al., 2018; Micozzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2018 and Micozzi et al., 2017.

claim: K. pneumoniae 43816 strain robustly infects lungs eliciting a strong innate immune response through rapid and concurrent recruitment of neutrophils and iMOs to the infected lungs.
source: In murine models of infection, the K. pneumoniae 43816 strain robustly infects lungs eliciting a strong innate immune response through rapid and concurrent recruitment of neutrophils and iMOs to the infected lungs (Lawlor et al., 2005; Xiong et al., 2015; Cai et al., 2010; Batra et al., 2012; Sharma et al., 2014; Ye et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Neutrophils are the first responder cell type for fighting against invading pathogens.
source: Neutrophils are the first responder cell type for fighting against invading pathogens, however, their activation is tightly regulated to prevent severe tissue damage that have been correlated with several autoimmune and inflammatory diseases (Mócsai, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mócsai, 2013 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Neutrophil activation is tightly regulated to prevent severe tissue damage that have been correlated with several autoimmune and inflammatory diseases.
source: Neutrophils are the first responder cell type for fighting against invading pathogens, however, their activation is tightly regulated to prevent severe tissue damage that have been correlated with several autoimmune and inflammatory diseases (Mócsai, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mócsai, 2013.

claim: At the site of infection, neutrophils can bind to pathogens leading to the activation of various killing mechanisms, including phagocytosis, generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), degranulation, and release of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).
source: At the site of infection, neutrophils can bind to pathogens leading to the activation of various killing mechanisms, including phagocytosis, generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), degranulation, and release of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) (Futosi et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2017; Mócsai, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The K. pneumoniae capsule decreases bacterial binding and internalization.
source: Although the K. pneumoniae capsule decreases bacterial binding and internalization (Regueiro et al., 2006; March et al., 2013), ROS, degranulation, NETs, and cytokine production have all been implicated in host defense against K. pneumoniae (Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa, 2019; Chen et al., 2016; Hirche et al., 2005; Ivin et al., 2017; Paczosa et al., 2020; Papayannopoulos et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Regueiro et al., 2006 and March et al., 2013.

claim: ROS, degranulation, NETs, and cytokine production have all been implicated in host defense against K. pneumoniae.
source: Although the K. pneumoniae capsule decreases bacterial binding and internalization (Regueiro et al., 2006; March et al., 2013), ROS, degranulation, NETs, and cytokine production have all been implicated in host defense against K. pneumoniae (Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa, 2019; Chen et al., 2016; Hirche et al., 2005; Ivin et al., 2017; Paczosa et al., 2020; Papayannopoulos et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Patients with Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) are unable to make ROS and are susceptible to Klebsiella infections.
source: The importance of ROS in host protection is highlighted in the setting of Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), a disease characterized by genetic mutations in the NADPH oxidase, where patients are unable to make ROS and are susceptible to Klebsiella infections (Wolach et al., 2017; Bortoletto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wolach et al., 2017 and Bortoletto et al., 2015.

claim: Mice with defective ROS production (Cybb-/-) have a higher bacterial burden than wild-type mice during K. pneumoniae lung infection.
source: Furthermore, mice with defective ROS production (Cybb-/-) have a higher bacterial burden than wild-type mice during K. pneumoniae lung infection (Paczosa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paczosa et al., 2020 and data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Receptor-mediated ROS production in neutrophils is driven by signal-transduction pathways that activate components of the NADPH oxidase complex.
source: Receptor-mediated ROS production in neutrophils is driven by signal-transduction pathways that activate components of the NADPH oxidase complex (Nguyen et al., 2017; Futosi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 2017 and Futosi et al., 2013.

claim: Signaling through integrin, mincle receptors, G-protein couple receptors (GPCRs) and toll-like receptors (TLRs) are critical for protection against K. pneumoniae infection.
source: Work in mice suggests that signaling through integrin, mincle receptors, G-protein couple receptors (GPCRs) and toll-like receptors (TLRs) are critical for protection against K. pneumoniae infection (Teng et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2014; Sharma et al., 2017; Regueiro et al., 2006; Galvão et al., 2018; Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: SKAP2 is required for integrin-mediated ROS production, adhesion, and migration to sterile inflammatory sites through its interaction with mediators of actin rearrangement.
source: SKAP2, a cytosolic adaptor protein, is required for integrin-mediated ROS production, adhesion, and migration to sterile inflammatory sites through its interaction with mediators of actin rearrangement (Alenghat et al., 2012; Boras et al., 2017; Shimamura et al., 2013; Tanaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: SKAP2 is a target for inactivation by bacterial virulence factors.
source: SKAP2 is also a target for inactivation by bacterial virulence factors, suggesting that it plays a key role in host defenses against infections (Black et al., 2000; Rolán et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Black et al., 2000 and Rolán et al., 2013.

claim: The Skap2 gene has been identified as a risk locus for Type 1 Diabetes and Crohn's disease in humans.
source: In humans, the Skap2 gene has been identified as a risk locus for Type 1 Diabetes, and Crohn's disease (Jostins et al., 2012; Barrett et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jostins et al., 2012 and Barrett et al., 2009.

claim: In resting cells, SKAP2 is thought to exist in an autoinhibitory conformation as a homodimer that is constitutively bound to PRAM-1 in neutrophils.
source: In resting cells, SKAP2 is thought to exist in an autoinhibitory conformation as a homodimer that is constitutively bound to PRAM-1 in neutrophils (Moog-Lutz et al., 2001; Rolán et al., 2013), or its homolog, ADAP, in other immune cells (Liu et al., 1998; Marie-Cardine et al., 1998; Black et al., 2000; Ophir et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Upon receptor activation, SKAP2 changes to an active conformation that is localized to the plasma membrane.
source: Upon receptor activation, SKAP2 changes to an active conformation that is localized to the plasma membrane, which allows it to interact other effector proteins including Src Family Kinases (SFKs) (Bureau et al., 2018; Marie-Cardine et al., 1998; Liu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Activated SKAP proteins can relay information from receptors to focal adhesion kinases (FAK1/Pyk2) to other cytoskeletal mediators.
source: In addition, activated SKAP proteins can relay information from receptors to focal adhesion kinases (FAK1/Pyk2) to other cytoskeletal mediators (Ménasché et al., 2007; Boras et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2017; Ophir et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: By 24 hr, infected WT mice lost 2% of their body weight.
source: Consistent with prior studies, by 24 hr, infected WT mice lost 2% of their body weight, and K. pneumoniae reached on average 106 cfu with a 5-fold increase in neutrophil presence in the infected lungs (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: K. pneumoniae reached on average 10^6 cfu in WT mice by 24 hr.
source: Consistent with prior studies, by 24 hr, infected WT mice lost 2% of their body weight, and K. pneumoniae reached on average 106 cfu with a 5-fold increase in neutrophil presence in the infected lungs (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There was a 5-fold increase in neutrophil presence in the infected lungs of WT mice by 24 hr.
source: Consistent with prior studies, by 24 hr, infected WT mice lost 2% of their body weight, and K. pneumoniae reached on average 106 cfu with a 5-fold increase in neutrophil presence in the infected lungs (Figure 1A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Skap2-/- mice lost significantly more body weight than the WT cohort at 24 hpi.
source: However, Skap2-/- mice lost significantly more body weight than the WT cohort at 24 hpi (Figure 1A) and had significantly higher bacterial loads in their lungs at 16 and 24 hpi (Figure 1B), indicating that Skap2-/- mice are less competent at controlling K. pneumoniae infection.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Skap2-/- mice had significantly higher bacterial loads in their lungs at 16 and 24 hpi.
source: However, Skap2-/- mice lost significantly more body weight than the WT cohort at 24 hpi (Figure 1A) and had significantly higher bacterial loads in their lungs at 16 and 24 hpi (Figure 1B), indicating that Skap2-/- mice are less competent at controlling K. pneumoniae infection.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Skap2-/- mice are less competent at controlling K. pneumoniae infection.
source: However, Skap2-/- mice lost significantly more body weight than the WT cohort at 24 hpi (Figure 1A) and had significantly higher bacterial loads in their lungs at 16 and 24 hpi (Figure 1B), indicating that Skap2-/- mice are less competent at controlling K. pneumoniae infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased weight loss and bacterial burden in Skap2-/- mice.

claim: Neutrophils were detected at comparable levels in WT and Skap2-/- lungs, bone marrow as well as bronchoalveolar lavage of infected mice.
source: The increase in bacterial burden did not appear to be due to differences in the numbers of neutrophils (CD11b+ Ly6Ghi) because neutrophils were detected at comparable levels in WT and Skap2-/- lungs, bone marrow as well as bronchoalveolar lavage of infected mice (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: There was no difference in alveolar macrophages, resident monocytes, or dendritic cells in the lungs of K. pneumoniae-infected WT and Skap2-/- mice.
source: In addition, there was no difference in alveolar macrophages (CD11bint CD11chi), resident monocytes (CD11b+ Gr1lo), or dendritic cells (CD11bhi CD11chi) in the lungs of K. pneumoniae-infected WT and Skap2-/- mice (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–J.

claim: Histological examination showed extensive leukocyte infiltration in both the WT and Skap2-/- infected lungs.
source: Histological examination showed extensive leukocyte infiltration in both the WT and Skap2-/- infected lungs supporting the flow cytometry data (Figure 1D–L, black arrows).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1D–L.

claim: Some infected Skap2-/- lungs (2/5 lungs) had lesions with cellular destruction and uncontrolled bacterial growth surrounded by sparse leukocyte infiltration.
source: Furthermore, some infected Skap2-/- lungs (2/5 lungs) had lesions with cellular destruction and uncontrolled bacterial growth surrounded by sparse leukocyte infiltration (Figure 1K–L, blue arrows).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1K–L.

claim: At 24 hpi, C57BL/6 Skap2-/- mice had a significant increase in bacterial burden compared to C57BL/6 and heterozygous littermates.
source: At 24 hpi, C57BL/6 Skap2-/- mice had a significant increase in bacterial burden compared to C57BL/6 and heterozygous littermates (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Comparable numbers of neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes were detected in C57BL/6, C57BL/6 Skap2-/-, and heterozygous littermates.
source: In general, comparable numbers of neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes were detected in all three strains (Figure 1N; Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–N) although the percent of neutrophils recovered in C57Bl/6 Skap2-/- mice was higher (Figure 1N)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–N.

claim: The percent of neutrophils recovered in C57Bl/6 Skap2-/- mice was higher.
source: In general, comparable numbers of neutrophils and inflammatory monocytes were detected in all three strains (Figure 1N; Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–N) although the percent of neutrophils recovered in C57Bl/6 Skap2-/- mice was higher (Figure 1N)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: WT recipient mice reconstituted with Skap2-/- BM had significantly more K. pneumoniae in contrast to WT mice transplanted with WT BM.
source: WT recipient mice reconstituted with Skap2-/- BM had significantly more K. pneumoniae in contrast to WT mice transplanted with WT BM (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Skap2-/- recipients with WT BM cells had significantly decreased K. pneumoniae in their lungs as compared to Skap2-/- hosts that received Skap2-/- BM cells.
source: Conversely, Skap2-/- recipients with WT BM cells had significantly decreased K. pneumoniae in their lungs as compared to Skap2-/- hosts that received Skap2-/- BM cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The differences in bacterial burdens in bone marrow chimeras were not due to differences in numbers of neutrophils.
source: The differences in bacterial burdens were not due to differences in numbers of neutrophils as equivalent numbers were recovered among all four groups of mice (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Fewer inflammatory monocytes were detected in Skap2-/- recipients regardless of BM cell donor.
source: While fewer inflammatory monocytes (iMOs) were detected in Skap2-/- recipients regardless of BM cell donor, the difference did not correlate with bacterial load (Figure 2B,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: The difference in inflammatory monocytes did not correlate with bacterial load.
source: While fewer inflammatory monocytes (iMOs) were detected in Skap2-/- recipients regardless of BM cell donor, the difference did not correlate with bacterial load (Figure 2B,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bacterial burden was rescued by WT BM despite lower iMO numbers.

claim: Skap2 expression in BM-derived immune cells is required to contain K. pneumoniae growth during lung infection.
source: Combined, these data indicate Skap2 expression in BM-derived immune cells is required to contain K. pneumoniae growth during lung infection, and that Skap2 expression in cells that are not derived from the marrow do not contribute to this phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Skap2 expression in cells that are not derived from the marrow do not contribute to K. pneumoniae control.
source: Combined, these data indicate Skap2 expression in BM-derived immune cells is required to contain K. pneumoniae growth during lung infection, and that Skap2 expression in cells that are not derived from the marrow do not contribute to this phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow chimera experiments showing that recipient genotype does not affect bacterial burden.

claim: Significantly more bacteria were recovered from the lungs of neutrophil-depleted WT mice.
source: While the K. pneumoniae burden in iMOs-depleted WT mice was similar to vehicle-treated mice, significantly more bacteria were recovered from the lungs of neutrophil-depleted WT mice (Figure 2E) confirming the importance of neutrophils in host defense (Ye et al., 2001; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The K. pneumoniae burden in iMOs-depleted WT mice was similar to vehicle-treated mice.
source: While the K. pneumoniae burden in iMOs-depleted WT mice was similar to vehicle-treated mice, significantly more bacteria were recovered from the lungs of neutrophil-depleted WT mice (Figure 2E) confirming the importance of neutrophils in host defense (Ye et al., 2001; Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The neutrophil-depleted WT mice had similarly high bacterial burdens as Skap2-/- mice.
source: The neutrophil-depleted WT mice had similarly high bacterial burdens as Skap2-/- mice (Figure 2E), and the depletion of Skap2-/- mice of neutrophils or iMOs did not increase their bacterial burden suggesting that protection against K. pneumoniae infection is SKAP2-dependent (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The depletion of Skap2-/- mice of neutrophils or iMOs did not increase their bacterial burden.
source: The neutrophil-depleted WT mice had similarly high bacterial burdens as Skap2-/- mice (Figure 2E), and the depletion of Skap2-/- mice of neutrophils or iMOs did not increase their bacterial burden suggesting that protection against K. pneumoniae infection is SKAP2-dependent (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Protection against K. pneumoniae infection is SKAP2-dependent.
source: The neutrophil-depleted WT mice had similarly high bacterial burdens as Skap2-/- mice (Figure 2E), and the depletion of Skap2-/- mice of neutrophils or iMOs did not increase their bacterial burden suggesting that protection against K. pneumoniae infection is SKAP2-dependent (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neutrophil depletion in Skap2-/- mice does not further increase bacterial burden.

claim: Skap2-/- mice that received WT BM and were then depleted of neutrophils with α-Ly6G showed an increase in bacterial load.
source: Skap2-/- mice that received WT BM and were then depleted of neutrophils with α-Ly6G showed an increase in bacterial load and that burden was similar to those in Skap2-/- mice that received Skap2-/- neutrophils (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: α-CCR2-treated mice had a similar bacterial burden as PBS-treated mice.
source: By contrast, α-CCR2-treated mice had a similar bacterial burden as PBS-treated mice (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Neutrophils cannot control K. pneumoniae 43816 infection in the absence of SKAP2 in the hematopoietic compartment.
source: Together, these data indicate that neutrophils cannot control K. pneumoniae 43816 infection in the absence of SKAP2 in the hematopoietic compartment.
evidence: This is supported by depletion experiments shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: The uncontrolled K. pneumoniae growth may occur because of defects in the antimicrobial functions of Skap2-/- neutrophils at the site of infection.
source: As Skap2-/- neutrophils are present in infected tissues (Figure 1D,J,N; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D), the uncontrolled K. pneumoniae growth may occur because of defects in the antimicrobial functions of Skap2-/- neutrophils at the site of infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of neutrophils but increased bacterial burden in Skap2-/- mice.

claim: Neither Skap2-/- BM nor DIV neutrophils produced ROS following exposure to K. pneumoniae.
source: In contrast to WT BM and DIV neutrophils, neither Skap2-/- BM nor DIV neutrophils produced ROS following exposure to K. pneumoniae (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is supported by isoluminol-chemiluminescence assay data shown in Figure 5A–B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The loss of K. pneumoniae-stimulated ROS production was not due to a defect in bacterial-binding.
source: The loss of K. pneumoniae-stimulated ROS production was not due to a defect in bacterial-binding as WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils bound GFP-labeled K. pneumoniae equivalently when assessed by flow cytometry following both 15- and 30 min incubations (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils bound GFP-labeled K. pneumoniae equivalently when assessed by flow cytometry following both 15- and 30 min incubations.
source: The loss of K. pneumoniae-stimulated ROS production was not due to a defect in bacterial-binding as WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils bound GFP-labeled K. pneumoniae equivalently when assessed by flow cytometry following both 15- and 30 min incubations (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SKAP2 was important for ROS production after infection with Y. pseudotuberculosis ΔyscF.
source: Finally, SKAP2 was important for ROS production after infection with another gram-negative bacterial strain, a type 3 deficient Y. pseudotuberculosis strain, ΔyscF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ROS assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Skap2-/- neutrophils are defective in triggering the signaling cascade(s) required for ROS after K. pneumoniae binding to surface receptors.
source: In summary, Skap2-/- neutrophils are defective in triggering the signaling cascade(s) required for ROS after K. pneumoniae binding to surface receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the abolishment of ROS production despite normal bacterial binding.

claim: Pretreatment with PP2, R406, Ibrutinib, U-73122, and Go6983 abolished ROS production after K. pneumoniae infection compared to vehicle-pretreated neutrophils.
source: Pretreatment with PP2, R406, Ibrutinib, U-73122, and Go6983 abolished ROS production after K. pneumoniae infection compared to vehicle-pretreated neutrophils (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by inhibitor studies shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Only pretreatment with Go6983 blocked ROS after PMA exposure.
source: As expected, only pretreatment with Go6983 blocked ROS after PMA exposure.
evidence: This is supported by inhibitor studies shown in Figure 5E.

claim: U73433, an U73122 analog that does not target PLCγ, did not block K. pneumoniae- and PMA-induced ROS.
source: U73433, an U73122 analog that does not target PLCγ, did not block K. pneumoniae- and PMA-induced ROS (Figure 5E; Rolán et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by inhibitor studies shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SFKs, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, and PKC are each necessary for K. pneumoniae-activated ROS production.
source: This suggests SFKs, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, and PKC are each necessary for K. pneumoniae-activated ROS production.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibitor studies showing that blocking each of these proteins abolishes ROS production.

claim: Infection with K. pneumoniae induced phosphorylation of SFKs and Syk to levels 2–5-fold higher than in unstimulated neutrophils.
source: Infection with K. pneumoniae induced phosphorylation of SFKs (pSFK) and Syk (pSFK) to levels 2–5-fold higher than in unstimulated neutrophils (Figure 5F–I; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F–I and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Pyk2 was phosphorylated in response to K. pneumoniae stimulation.
source: In addition, proline-rich tyrosine kinase 2 (Pyk2), which is a tyrosine kinase that functions downstream of SFKs and Syk to mediate ROS production (Kamen et al., 2011; Zhao and Bokoch, 2005), was phosphorylated in response to K. pneumoniae stimulation (Figure 5K–L; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5K–L and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Signaling circuit(s) containing SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 were activated in neutrophils following receptor binding of K. pneumoniae.
source: Thus, signaling circuit(s) containing SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 were activated in neutrophils following receptor binding of K. pneumoniae.
evidence: This is inferred from the phosphorylation of these kinases after K. pneumoniae stimulation.

claim: While SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 phosphorylation were all slightly induced in Skap2-/- neutrophils, the level of induction was often significantly reduced as compared to WT neutrophils.
source: While SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 phosphorylation were all slightly induced in Skap2-/- neutrophils, the level of induction was often significantly reduced as compared to WT neutrophils (Figure 5F–L; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F–L and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Stimulation of FcγRs resulted in the phosphorylation for SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 to similar levels in both WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils.
source: To determine if the reduction in phosphorylation was due to decreased cell viability, Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils were also stimulated with IC as a control. Stimulation of FcγRs resulted in the phosphorylation for SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 to similar levels in both WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils (Figure 5F,H,K and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F, H, K and Supplementary file 1.

claim: SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 are required for K. pneumoniae-stimulated ROS production.
source: Collectively, these results show that SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 are required for K. pneumoniae-stimulated ROS production, and that the loss of SKAP2 prevents full phosphorylation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 after K. pneumoniae stimulation such that neutrophils are unable to generate ROS production.
evidence: This is supported by inhibitor studies and phosphorylation data.

claim: The loss of SKAP2 prevents full phosphorylation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 after K. pneumoniae stimulation such that neutrophils are unable to generate ROS production.
source: Collectively, these results show that SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 are required for K. pneumoniae-stimulated ROS production, and that the loss of SKAP2 prevents full phosphorylation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 after K. pneumoniae stimulation such that neutrophils are unable to generate ROS production.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing reduced phosphorylation in Skap2-/- neutrophils and abolished ROS production.

claim: Supernatants from WT and Skap2-/- K. pneumoniae-infected lungs had equivalent levels of MMP-9 and ELA2 at 16 and 24 hpi.
source: Supernatants from WT and Skap2-/- K. pneumoniae-infected lungs had equivalent levels of MMP-9 and ELA2 in Skap2-/- at 16 and 24 hpi as detected by ELISA (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: The increased susceptibility of Skap2-/- mice was not due to defects in degranulation.
source: This suggests that the increased in susceptibility of Skap2-/- mice was not due to defects in degranulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the equivalent levels of degranulation markers in WT and Skap2-/- mice.

claim: K. pneumoniae 43816 was recovered on average at less than 0.01% in WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils.
source: Using a more sensitive gentamicin protection assay (Walker et al., 2019), K. pneumoniae 43816 was recovered on average at less than 0.01% in WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils, while a non-encapsulated (ΔcpsB) K. pneumoniae strain was recovered at approximately 0.05% (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by gentamicin protection assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A non-encapsulated (ΔcpsB) K. pneumoniae strain was recovered at approximately 0.05% in WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils.
source: Using a more sensitive gentamicin protection assay (Walker et al., 2019), K. pneumoniae 43816 was recovered on average at less than 0.01% in WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils, while a non-encapsulated (ΔcpsB) K. pneumoniae strain was recovered at approximately 0.05% (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by gentamicin protection assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils were able to phagocytose Yersinia pseudotuberculosis YPIII ΔyscNU strain.
source: This low level was not due to a defect in phagocytosis of DIV neutrophils as WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils were able to phagocytose Yersinia pseudotuberculosis YPIII ΔyscNU strain, a strain that is susceptible to phagocytosis (Balada-Llasat and Mecsas, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by gentamicin protection assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils phagocytosed 20% and 10% of ΔyscNU, respectively.
source: WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils phagocytosed 20% and 10% of ΔyscNU, respectively (Figure 4C), suggesting that phagocytosis of this Y. pseudotuberculosis strain is partially dependent on SKAP2.
evidence: This is supported by gentamicin protection assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Phagocytosis of Y. pseudotuberculosis ΔyscNU strain is partially dependent on SKAP2.
source: WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils phagocytosed 20% and 10% of ΔyscNU, respectively (Figure 4C), suggesting that phagocytosis of this Y. pseudotuberculosis strain is partially dependent on SKAP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced phagocytosis in Skap2-/- neutrophils compared to WT.

claim: The K. pneumoniae 43816 strain is resistant to neutrophil phagocytosis regardless of SKAP2 expression.
source: Although we observed low level of phagocytosis of K. pneumoniae 43816, the SKAP2-mediated defect in phagocytosis might be more prominent when challenged with other K. pneumoniae isolates. Combined, these results indicate that the K. pneumoniae 43816 strain is resistant to neutrophil phagocytosis regardless of SKAP2 expression, but can elicit SKAP2-independent degranulation during infection.
evidence: This is supported by the low and equivalent phagocytosis levels in WT and Skap2-/- neutrophils.

claim: K. pneumoniae 43816 can elicit SKAP2-independent degranulation during infection.
source: Although we observed low level of phagocytosis of K. pneumoniae 43816, the SKAP2-mediated defect in phagocytosis might be more prominent when challenged with other K. pneumoniae isolates. Combined, these results indicate that the K. pneumoniae 43816 strain is resistant to neutrophil phagocytosis regardless of SKAP2 expression, but can elicit SKAP2-independent degranulation during infection.
evidence: This is supported by the equivalent degranulation levels in WT and Skap2-/- mice.

claim: Degranulation in Skap2-/- mice was not sufficient to control K. pneumoniae burden in the absence of ROS.
source: However, we found that despite equivalent levels of ELA2, degranulation in Skap2-/- mice was not sufficient to control K. pneumoniae burden in the absence of ROS, indicating that neutrophil ROS and degranulation may cooperate in containing K. pneumoniae infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased bacterial burden in Skap2-/- mice despite normal degranulation.

claim: Neutrophil ROS and degranulation may cooperate in containing K. pneumoniae infection.
source: However, we found that despite equivalent levels of ELA2, degranulation in Skap2-/- mice was not sufficient to control K. pneumoniae burden in the absence of ROS, indicating that neutrophil ROS and degranulation may cooperate in containing K. pneumoniae infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that degranulation alone is insufficient for bacterial control.

claim: The pathways of ROS production are distinct from signaling pathways regulating degranulation in murine neutrophils after K. pneumoniae infection.
source: Since degranulation occurred normally in Skap2-/- lungs, the pathways of ROS production are distinct from signaling pathways regulating degranulation in murine neutrophils after K. pneumoniae infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ROS is abolished while degranulation is normal in Skap2-/- neutrophils.

claim: When plated onto surfaces coated with poly-RGD, WT BM and DIV neutrophils released superoxide, while Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils did not.
source: When plated onto surfaces coated with poly-RGD, an engineered polypeptide containing multiple copies of the integrin binding motif, WT BM and DIV neutrophils released superoxide, while Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils did not (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is supported by cytochrome C reduction assay data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: The loss in integrin-mediated ROS production was not due to defects in the NADPH oxidase itself.
source: The loss in integrin-mediated ROS production was not due to defects in the NADPH oxidase itself, as Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils robustly released ROS when stimulated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA), which bypasses receptor-mediated signaling pathways and activates NADPH oxidase via protein kinase C (PKC) (Dang et al., 2001; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by PMA-stimulated ROS production data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils robustly released ROS when stimulated with PMA.
source: The loss in integrin-mediated ROS production was not due to defects in the NADPH oxidase itself, as Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils robustly released ROS when stimulated with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA), which bypasses receptor-mediated signaling pathways and activates NADPH oxidase via protein kinase C (PKC) (Dang et al., 2001; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by PMA-stimulated ROS production data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After stimulation of Fcγ receptors by IgG immune complexes (IC), WT and Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils robustly produced ROS.
source: By contrast, after stimulation of Fcγ receptors by IgG immune complexes (IC), WT and Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils robustly produced ROS (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is supported by cytochrome C reduction assay data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils consistently released 60–80% as much ROS as compared to levels seen in comparable WT neutrophils after IC stimulation.
source: Skap2-/- BM and DIV neutrophils consistently released 60–80% as much ROS as compared to levels seen in comparable WT neutrophils.
evidence: This is supported by cytochrome C reduction assay data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: IC-stimulated ROS is partially dependent on SKAP2.
source: This indicates IC-stimulated ROS is partially dependent on SKAP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced but not abolished ROS production in Skap2-/- neutrophils after IC stimulation.

claim: WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils expressed similar levels of integrin and Fcγ receptors as measured by CD11b and CD16 expression, respectively.
source: Differences in ROS production were not due to differences in surface marker expression levels as WT and Skap2-/- DIV neutrophils expressed similar levels of integrin and Fcγ receptors as measured by CD11b and CD16 expression, respectively, by flow cytometry (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3G–J.

claim: WT and Skap2-/- DIVs phenocopy primary BM neutrophils both morphologically and functionally.
source: Combined, these results indicate WT and Skap2-/- DIVs phenocopy primary BM neutrophils both morphologically and functionally and are a useful tool to investigate how SKAP2 modulates K. pneumoniae-induced neutrophil responses.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis and functional ROS assays comparing DIV and BM neutrophils.

claim: A functional NADPH complex can assemble in Skap2-/- neutrophils.
source: Furthermore, these data suggest that a functional NADPH complex can assemble in Skap2-/- neutrophils and that SKAP2 is required for receptor-activated signaling pathways downstream of integrin receptors, but not Fcγ receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the robust ROS production after PMA stimulation in Skap2-/- neutrophils.

claim: SKAP2 is required for receptor-activated signaling pathways downstream of integrin receptors, but not Fcγ receptors.
source: Furthermore, these data suggest that a functional NADPH complex can assemble in Skap2-/- neutrophils and that SKAP2 is required for receptor-activated signaling pathways downstream of integrin receptors, but not Fcγ receptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the abolished integrin-mediated ROS but partially preserved FcγR-mediated ROS in Skap2-/- neutrophils.

claim: Following K. pneumoniae infection, activation of receptors leads to the activation of PI3K and the generation of PIP3, resulting in PIP3-mediated SKAP2 activation and membrane localization.
source: Following K. pneumoniae infection, activation of receptors, like GPCRs recognizing N-formylated bacterial proteins or mincle recognizing bacterial lectins, leads to the activation of phosphoinositide 3 kinase (PI3K) and the generation of phosphatidylinositol [3,4,5]-triphosphate (PIP3), resulting in PIP3-mediated SKAP2 activation and membrane localization (Figure 6A–B; Futosi et al., 2013; Swanson et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2014; Alenghat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: The activated (open) phosphorylated SKAP2 complex can bind to and enhance phosphorylation of SFKs shifting their active/inactive equilibrium to more active forms and leading to Syk activation.
source: The activated (open) phosphorylated SKAP2 complex can then bind to and enhance phosphorylation of SFKs shifting their active/inactive equilibrium to more active forms and leading to Syk activation (Figure 6B; Marie-Cardine et al., 1998; Bureau et al., 2018; Kouroku et al., 1998; Lowell, 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: SKAP2 can directly interact with SFKs.
source: This is supported by previous biochemical and pull-down studies showing that SKAP2 can directly interact with SFKs (Bureau et al., 2018; Liu et al., 1998; Wang and Rudd, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bureau et al., 2018, Liu et al., 1998, and Wang and Rudd, 2008.

claim: SFKs and Syk may directly associate with and activate Pyk2.
source: SFKs and Syk may directly associate with and activate Pyk2, as observed in response to GPCRs, integrin, TNFα, and/or Salmonella stimulation (Dikic et al., 1996; Evangelista et al., 2007; Han et al., 2003; Mócsai et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dikic et al., 1996, Evangelista et al., 2007, Han et al., 2003, and Mócsai et al., 2002.

claim: SKAP2 may interact with Pyk2 signaling complex directly or indirectly through their association with Sirpα.
source: Furthermore, SKAP2 may interact with Pyk2 signaling complex directly or indirectly through their association with Sirpα (Raab et al., 2017; Alenghat et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on cited literature.

claim: Skap2-/- mice have normal levels of circulating neutrophils.
source: Skap2-/- mice have normal levels of circulating neutrophils and Skap2-/- neutrophils were present in K. pneumoniae-infected lungs at a similar, and sometimes higher, levels as WT neutrophils (Figure 1C–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and (Togni et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data and citation to Togni et al., 2005.

claim: Skap2-/- myeloid cells have impaired recruitment and migration into tissues during sterile inflammation.
source: However, prior studies revealed that Skap2-/- myeloid cells, including neutrophils, have impaired recruitment and migration into tissues during sterile inflammation (Tanaka et al., 2016; Boras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tanaka et al., 2016 and Boras et al., 2017.

claim: Migration to sterile, but not infectious sites, may require SKAP2.
source: This suggests that migration to sterile, but not infectious sites, may require SKAP2, which is consistent with findings with Syk.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Skap2-/- neutrophils are present in infected lungs but have impaired migration to sterile sites.

claim: Syk is required for neutrophil migration in an inflammatory model but not during bacterial infection.
source: Syk is required for neutrophil migration in an inflammatory model but not during bacterial infection (Zarbock et al., 2007; Frommhold et al., 2007; Van Ziffle and Lowell, 2009; Schymeinsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: ROS production can increase myeloid cell death.
source: This result could arise because ROS production can increase myeloid cell death (Coxon et al., 1996; Geering and Simon, 2011; Geering et al., 2011), and thus, defects in ROS production by Skap2-/- neutrophils could contribute to higher survival and accumulation in infected murine lungs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coxon et al., 1996, Geering and Simon, 2011, and Geering et al., 2011.

claim: Defects in ROS production by Skap2-/- neutrophils could contribute to higher survival and accumulation in infected murine lungs.
source: This result could arise because ROS production can increase myeloid cell death (Coxon et al., 1996; Geering and Simon, 2011; Geering et al., 2011), and thus, defects in ROS production by Skap2-/- neutrophils could contribute to higher survival and accumulation in infected murine lungs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed neutrophil levels in Skap2-/- mice.

claim: There exist significant differences between mice and humans in the immune response to infection.
source: Murine models of infection have been helpful in illuminating K. pneumoniae infection biology, however, there exist significant differences between mice and humans in the immune response to infection, including disparities in structural anatomy, circulating neutrophil counts, surface receptors, and signaling cascades, among others (Mizgerd and Skerrett, 2008; Mestas and Hughes, 2004; Condliffe et al., 2005; Hajjar et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2016; Bagaitkar et al., 2012; Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: It is unknown if SKAP2 plays a role in mediating the human neutrophil response to K. pneumoniae infection.
source: Thus, to date it is unknown if SKAP2 plays a role in mediating the human neutrophil response to K. pneumoniae infection.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the manuscript.

claim: Skap2 has 9 transcripts and at least 50 exonic variants that have been reported in the human population.
source: Skap2 has 9 transcripts and at least 50 exonic variants that have been reported in the human population, however, their functional consequences, if any, remains unclear (Cunningham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cunningham et al., 2019.

claim: The functional consequences of Skap2 variants in humans remain unclear.
source: Skap2 has 9 transcripts and at least 50 exonic variants that have been reported in the human population, however, their functional consequences, if any, remains unclear (Cunningham et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the manuscript.

claim: Genome-wide analyses of K. pneumoniae clinical isolates have shown extensive genetic diversity, virulence factors, and pathogenicity.
source: Genome-wide analyses of K. pneumoniae clinical isolates have shown extensive genetic diversity, virulence factors, and pathogenicity (Holt et al., 2015; Deleo et al., 2014; Agard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holt et al., 2015, Deleo et al., 2014, and Agard et al., 2019.

claim: Neutrophils are not the major player in host defenses against all strains of K. pneumoniae, including some multi-drug resistant clinical isolates.
source: Furthermore, since neutrophils are not the major player in host defenses against all strains of K. pneumoniae, including some multi-drug resistant clinical isolates (Xiong et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2015; Broug-Holub et al., 1997; Greenberger et al., 1996), future studies can use these K. pneumoniae strains to probe the role of SKAP2 in neutrophils as well as other hematopoietic cells during K. pneumoniae infections.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiong et al., 2016, Xiong et al., 2015, Broug-Holub et al., 1997, and Greenberger et al., 1996.

claim: Neutrophils and their production of ROS play a dual role in host health in many disease states from acute infections to autoimmune diseases to cancer.
source: In summary, neutrophils and their production of ROS play a dual role in host health in many disease states from acute infections to autoimmune diseases to cancer (Hoffmann and Griffiths, 2018; Nguyen et al., 2017), and the crucial function of SKAP2-mediated ROS in murine neutrophils suggests that further analysis of the role of SKAP2 in human health warrants investigation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hoffmann and Griffiths, 2018 and Nguyen et al., 2017.

claim: The crucial function of SKAP2-mediated ROS in murine neutrophils suggests that further analysis of the role of SKAP2 in human health warrants investigation.
source: In summary, neutrophils and their production of ROS play a dual role in host health in many disease states from acute infections to autoimmune diseases to cancer (Hoffmann and Griffiths, 2018; Nguyen et al., 2017), and the crucial function of SKAP2-mediated ROS in murine neutrophils suggests that further analysis of the role of SKAP2 in human health warrants investigation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.
